entries.title: Justice Kagan Warns Supreme Court Rulings Are Fueling Polarization
entries.summary: The liberal-leaning justice said both political parties are "in a race to the bottom" with partisan gerrymanders.
entries.content:
By Lindsay Whitehurst

Justice Elena Kagan on Tuesday said voting and elections decisions from her conservative Supreme Court colleagues have helped make the country more politically polarized and less democratic.

In a speech two weeks before the pivotal midterm elections for control of Congress, the liberal-leaning justice sharply criticized how the majority’s rulings have affected the nation’s political environment.

“The court has kind of blinded itself to the very deleterious effect of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that does not work as well as it should,” she said during a talk before students and professors at Catholic University's law school in Washington, D.C.

She blasted rulings that weakened the Voting Rights Act and campaign finance regulations while opening the door for more partisan gerrymandering. She dissented from those decisions.

“Over the last couple of years especially, both political parties have been engaged in a race to the bottom in terms of doing these partisan gerrymanders, … making what I think is unfortunately a too polarized country even more so,” she said. “The people of America look around and think that all this money chasing all these political candidates is a nightmare, and they're right.”

The court’s majority, for its part, said in a 2019 ruling that courts drawing voting districts for maximum advantage is a political dispute and federal courts can’t step in. Conservatives have separately ruled that key campaign finance regulations violate the freedom of speech. This year, the court further narrowed protections in the Voting Rights Act, which had helped increase minority representation.

That helped feed a redistricting frenzy touched off by President Donald Trump, who is trying to hold on to the Republicans' slim House majorities in the November election.

Still, Kagan said it's unfair to say the majority reflexively supports the president. She pointed to key areas where the court has pushed back against Trump, including tariffs, birthright citizenship and mail ballots.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Trump’s Super PACs Have Spent More Than $238 Million Since September
entries.summary: The spending spree leaves the president’s PAC network with $189 million in reserves.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump’s super PAC network poured about $238 million into key congressional races from September through mid-October, new federal filings show.

The aggressive fall spending spree left MAGA Inc. and two related committees, No Going Back PAC and Safety and Affordability PAC, with a cumulative $189 million in reserves as of mid-October — just a few weeks after Trump claimed that he had raised close to $1 billion.

The disclosures came hours after Trump claimed on Truth Social that he had already spent more than $300 million helping Republicans ahead of the midterms and would likely spend $100 million more — figures that line up with what he said earlier this fall he anticipated spending.

Notable donors to the network of committees included real estate developer Steve Wynn, who gave $8 million; Blackstone CEO Stephen Schwarzman with $5 million; and Wisconsin billionaire Diane Hendricks, who tossed in $5 million.

GEO Reentry Services, a company associated with operating several U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities, gave MAGA Inc. $1 million, bringing its combined contributions to more than $4 million.

The Vapor Technology Association gave $300,000. The company donated those funds on Sept. 8, and then announced a seven-figure advertising campaign Sept. 22 urging Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to rewrite Food and Drug Administration rules regarding flavored vaping products.

Trump has crisscrossed the country in recent months, holding dozens of rallies to support Republicans in competitive races. But the blitz began mainly after fellow party members publicly and privately begged the president to get more involved, and he had largely held off from dedicating serious sums from his campaign coffers until September.

From January 2025 through August, MAGA Inc. had taken in $424.4 million and paid out $32.4 million, and only about $2.5 million was reported as independent spending to elect or defeat candidates. The PAC drew scrutiny from political analysts and some Republicans for drawing large sums without spending aggressively on races that could decide control of Congress come November.

By mid-September the three groups aligned with MAGA Inc. ramped up spending, scheduling about $138 million in advertising, mail and text messaging spending across about 50 races, although much of that total was aimed for advertising reserved for the weeks ahead.

By October, the Trump-led PACs were already being forced to make choices about which Republicans to keep helping. Politico reported on Oct. 12 that MAGA Inc. planned to pull spending from several House races, including Michigan’s 8th District, and focus on protecting Senate seats in Ohio, Alaska and Iowa, all states Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

Trump’s insistence that he controls the money raised by MAGA Inc. spurred a recent Federal Election Commission complaint alleging the president broke rules governing how elected officeholders can control PAC money. In August, he corrected a Punchbowl reporter who described MAGA Inc. as controlled by his allies.

“Not my allies,” he said. “I control it.”
entries.author: Gavin J. Quinton

entries.title: The State Department Is Pushing Out Senior Foreign Service Officers
entries.summary: The Trump administration is looking to replace long-tenured staff with more loyal personnel, current and former employees say.
entries.content:
The State Department is aggressively trying to force out its most senior foreign service officers, according to nine current and former staff, who suggested that Trump administration officials are seeking to cast aside veteran personnel who they view as standing in the way of their agenda.

At the same time, the current and former employees said, State is recruiting and promoting new staff who they view as more politically loyal.

“The State Department is trying to get people to quit,” said one current foreign service officer, who was granted anonymity out of fear or retribution.

This effort comes more than a year after the State Department carried out massive layoffs, hollowing out the United States’ international foreign service footprint. Those who have spent decades in the State Department have said the administration’s approach has weakened relationships abroad, and led to deficient leadership internally and less informed foreign policy decisions.

The department has shrunk the number of roles available to senior foreign servants by freezing positions or downgrading them to lower levels, the State Department personnel said.

Many top-ranked career staff have voluntarily headed to the exits as their careers are stalled. Top political staff at the department have directly asked some long-tenured personnel to retire, former employees said. They have reassigned other top career staff into the Administration Bureau, what employees consider to be a “purgatory” where employees' careers “go to die.”

“A whole lot of senior foreign service have left because there are no jobs for them,” a second current foreign service officer said.

The State Department, like the military, operates an “up-or-out” system, meaning staff could be forced out if they do not get promoted quickly enough.

The State Department laid off more than 1,300 employees last year. Senior foreign service officers were disproportionately targeted in those cuts.

Around 3,500 foreign service employees have left the State Department since President Donald Trump retook office, according to the American Foreign Service Association, and a majority of those were in the senior ranks or one level below. Departing employees who have gone through the mandatory retirement classes this year said their size had grown by orders of magnitude and the department has been forced to hold sessions more often.

Tommy Pigott, a State Department spokesperson, said The Washington Sun’s reporting validated the agency’s efforts.

"Those bureaucrats who are complaining to the press prove the point that they shouldn’t have, and can’t be, trusted with sensitive information,” Pigott said.

The department is seeking out politically aligned staff through other means. It has increasingly leaned on the Ben Franklin Fellowship — which a Trump-aligned group of current and former State officials founded in 2024 — to identify individuals to hire and promote, current and former staff said. Individuals aligned with the group are disproportionately in senior roles. Deputy Secretary Christopher Landau is one of the Ben Franklin Fellows.

“There are people who are supportive of what is happening,” said Kelly Adams-Smith, who ended her 28-year foreign service career after the Trump administration withdrew her nomination to serve as ambassador to Moldova. “They are finding, much to their surprise, very senior positions in the department.”

One person said they participated in an interview panel for a senior-level position and were told by someone close to political leadership that the process was just for show and it had been predetermined the job was going to a Ben Franklin Fellow.

Earlier this year, State awarded a $1 million, no-bid contract to a recruitment firm whose CEO has said more Christians should serve in government and hiring at the department had become too “woke.” State also added a “fidelity” section to the performance evaluation process, requiring managers to assess employees’ commitment to “completely aligning oneself and one’s team to the most current [U.S. government] goals.”

Outside the favored circles, the administration has made it more difficult for foreign service officers to climb the ranks. This fall’s bidding cycles — the process through which a large swath of the diplomatic corps find new assignments each year — have left staff with fewer senior positions available than ever before.

Roles that were typically set aside for senior foreign service officers, such as an embassy’s deputy chief of mission, have been downgraded to a lower rank. For the second year in a row, embassies have also received directives to freeze a certain number of positions. Additionally, Trump is setting aside an usually small number of ambassadorships for career staff — and nearly half of those roles remain vacant.

“It’s like musical chairs but taking chairs away faster so people wind up with nowhere to go,” said a State employee who recently left the department.

Even senior employees willing to serve in lower positions have been told they would not be selected for those roles, employees said.

The State Department confirmed that it was not prioritizing years of service for senior jobs.

The policy changes, political pressure and a wave of resignations are having a significant impact on U.S. diplomacy, the current and former staff said.

Employees now feel reluctant to offer their views on key matters, something staff described as historically fundamental to the nation’s diplomatic success. Doing so could endanger their chances of promotion or risk other efforts to sideline their careers, they said.

“People are afraid to speak out, to voice their opinions even if they believe their opinions need to be heard,” said one foreign service officer who recently left the department.

Newer employees with less experience and fewer relationships abroad are in critical positions, both because of who the Trump administration is selecting and more junior workers are less likely to feel financially secure enough to step down.

“Someone who can retire or is more economically secure is more likely to tell the emperor that the emperor has no clothes,” one of the recently departed foreign service officers said. “Junior people are more likely to just say yes.”

That will lead to less informed foreign policy decisions, the person said.

“Good policy depends on good information,” the former employee said. “If you’re not getting the good information because people are afraid to share, then you are likely to have bad policy.”

Adams-Smith noted that when experienced diplomats leave the department, the agency also loses their “networks of contacts” abroad.

She had planned to continue serving at State, but reversed course after she realized the administration was “not interested in expert advice.”

“There was no place for me and it was clear my expertise was not going to be valued or welcome,” Adams-Smith said. “With the way they were handling things, it was clear it was time to go.”

Pigott, the department spokesperson, said State is willing to hear advice from “patriotic Americans.”

"Secretary [Marco] Rubio values candid insights from patriotic Americans who have chosen to serve their country,” he said. “What we will not tolerate is people using their positions to actively undermine the duly elected president’s objectives.”

Another recently retired foreign service officer said that replacing long-tenured staff with greener employees will lead to a “10-year gap where you don’t have seasoned expertise in bilateral, multilateral and interagency contexts. That will be detrimental to American interests.”

A diplomat who recently left the department said the administration’s approach could soon lead to a crisis.

“Honest advice is not being rendered,” the former employee said. “At some point, god forbid, something is going to come back and bite them, and maybe all of us, in the behind.”
entries.author: Eric Katz

entries.title: Trump’s Campaigning in Traditional Republican Strongholds Isn’t Making His Party See Red
entries.summary: GOP strategists say they are largely happy with the president’s focus on shoring up turnout instead of contesting battleground races.
entries.content:
GREENVILLE, N.C. — President Donald Trump is doing what some didn’t expect: He’s crisscrossing the country to campaign for Republicans, spending his time — and his super PAC’s cash — to keep a blue wave from pulling the final two years of his presidency under.

The change in strategy, Trump said Tuesday night at a rally for Senate candidate Michael Whatley, was intentional.

“I'm doing something different,” he told the crowd. “I'm working like a dog, and I love being with you.”

Trump’s speech beneath a billowing American flag at a campaign rally in North Carolina was like so many others he’s given in recent weeks — one that wove together a tangle of seemingly unrelated threads rather than providing a targeted closing message for a crucial election. Instead of talking about rising consumer prices, he opined on what constitutes an attractive man, complained about election integrity and welcomed racing legend Richard Petty to talk about supporters being Trump’s “pit crew.”

But as the president storms the country to stump for candidates in the election’s closing days, his itinerary has largely focused on red states and featured nods of acknowledgment to the problems that have cratered his approval rating to historic lows and set the scene for a potential blue wave. Republicans are betting that Trump’s message matters less than his presence does.

“The rallies are working for the people that they need to work for: the base,” said Steve Bannon, Trump’s former chief strategist and the host of “War Room,” a podcast popular among Trump supporters.

Shoring up Republican turnout in traditionally red areas of the country, Bannon and other Republican operatives tell The Washington Sun, is how Trump can best serve his party during the home stretch. The president remains the best motivator for getting Republicans to vote, even as his broader popularity has faded. And with control of Congress hanging in the balance, juicing turnout is desperately needed.

“He’s firing up the base,” said Alan Powell, a Greenville-area resident at Trump’s rally Tuesday. “That’s what matters.”

Democratic candidates, super PACs and committees are pouring money into states, races and districts that Republicans won by significant margins in 2024. Democratic Senate candidates in Kansas, Nebraska and Alaska — states Trump won in 2024 by 16 percentage points, 20 points and 13 points, respectively — are leading or within striking distance of the Republican incumbents in recent polling. Democratic operatives say the party can win the Senate majority, an outcome considered almost unthinkable just two years ago.

“The problem is we’re gonna lose the House in red states,” said a conservative operative, who, like others in this story, spoke on the condition of anonymity to talk openly about campaign dynamics. “That’s fucked up.”
Trump 26289817352212 (8026x5350, AR: 1.50)Republicans believe Trump’s presence on the campaign trail is the best counter to Democratic momentum. Turnout in the midterms trends lower than in presidential election years, and that, Republican strategists say, allows Trump to affect the outcome by activating more of the people passionate enough to vote.

“The midterm elections are all about turnout, and there's no one who energizes and engages Republican voters like President Donald J. Trump,” said RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre. “Republicans are thinking outside the box to fight the typical midterm precedent.”

Representatives for the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Bannon pointed to an increase in the number of Trump’s plane-hangar rallies, likening them to the final stretch of his 2016 campaign.

“He identifies the way to do this is to get the base,” Bannon said, adding that he’s seen a demonstrable change in urgency among Trump’s most loyal voters over the past two weeks. “Not simply the vote, but to make the list for 10 people to get them out to start canvassing, calling the phone banks.”

Trump promised in September to spend the final month of the election on the road, stumping for Republican candidates. And he has. But instead of barnstorming traditional swing states, the president has spent more time bouncing across the comfortable confines of states that should be Trump Country — Alabama, Tennessee, Kansas, Ohio, Nebraska and Alaska among them.

Trump plans to visit South Carolina, Iowa and Florida before returning to Georgia this weekend and to Texas next week. He’ll also make a rare battleground stop in Michigan.

Even the stops in more competitive states and districts have landed in friendly regions. Dalton, Georgia, the site of his rambling rally on Friday, is nestled in the district Marjorie Taylor Greene represented before she left Congress. On Tuesday, Trump visited North Carolina’s 3rd District, which overwhelmingly elected Republican Rep. Greg Murphy in 2024.

Trump’s rare forays into battlegrounds have delighted Democrats and dismayed some Republicans.

“He should stick to the White House; he should just stay there,” one Republican operative in Georgia said about Trump’s visit. “All he’s doing is hurting Republicans.”

Asked about the same rally, a Georgia Democrat was gleeful.

“If Trump could come to Georgia every week, we’d invite him,” the operative said, adding that Trump’s presence could help deliver the gubernatorial race for Keisha Lance Bottoms to make her the state’s first Black governor.
Trump 26293856909032 (8210x4618, AR: 1.78)Any impact from Trump’s rallies isn’t likely to stem from his messaging. His speeches have been long, winding variations of the same talk he’s given for months: dire warnings of coming communism brought by Democrats, a defense of the ongoing Iran war and blaming his predecessor for high prices — all mixed with pleas to act like he is on the ballot, tepid praise for whichever Republicans he is stumping for and insults for those candidates’ Democratic opponents.

Specific, state-based messaging — like using the red meat of gun-control policies while rallying in Montana — has been rare. And operatives are OK with that.

“Trump usually provides a lot of different messages,” said Republican strategist Ron Bonjean, “but everyone's used to that.”

The goal, Bonjean added, is to generate enthusiasm among the MAGA base.

“If they feel better about going to the polls because they heard from President Trump directly, then that's a win,” he said.

Trump’s visit earlier this month to Tennessee, for example, was to Montgomery County, an area that state Rep. Jeremy Faison said has felt closer to purple than red this cycle.

“Strategically, he’s trying to fit in places like that that he knows he can hopefully turn out some red voters,” Faison said.

Trump said in a Tuesday social media post that he expects to spend over $400 million by Nov. 3, seemingly referring to spending from his affiliated super PACs. He added that $300 million has already been spent, including on advertising, voter turnout and rallies.

One Democratic operative said it was smart to focus on boosting turnout within Republican strongholds rather than risking alienating swing-state voters. It showed Trump is “reading the room,” they added.

But if Trump’s trips to Georgia, North Carolina and Michigan lead to more battleground rallies, that operative said they wouldn’t be sad. Another Democratic strategist took it even further after Trump’s rally in Kansas on Monday, where he was heckled by a protester screaming, “I fucking hate you!”

“If Trump wants to stay in Kansas for the next two weeks,” the strategist said, “I wouldn’t mind!”
entries.author: Ben T.N. Mause, Jasmine Wright
